right: Steeper slope → faster change
caption: Read the axes first. The secant averages over an interval; the tangent gives the instantaneous slope. Reactant disappearance rates use a minus sign.
alt: A falling reactant curve with a secant and a tangent, beside two product lines with different positive slopes. Schematic graphs, not measured data.

right: Surface area: exposed reaction sites
caption: These particle and solid models explain two rate factors. Temperature, catalyst and reactant identity also affect rate, as described in the section.
alt: Equal-sized boxes contain four or nine particles. A cube is divided into eight smaller cubes, increasing total exposed surface area without changing its total volume.

right: Activation energy and activated complex
caption: ClNO₂ is drawn as a connectivity sketch, not a Lewis structure. The energy profile is schematic: it does not supply measured energies for this reaction.
alt: An incoming chlorine atom approaches the bound chlorine of ClNO2. Beside it an energy barrier labels activation energy from reactants to the activated complex.

right: Catalyst: another pathway
caption: The horizontal axis is reaction progress, not time. A catalyst lowers the barrier without changing the reactant–product enthalpy difference.
alt: Exothermic energy curve labels forward activation energy and the negative enthalpy change. A second plot compares higher uncatalyzed and lower catalyzed barriers with identical endpoints.

left: Mechanism: steps sum to the reaction
right: Slow elementary step and rate law
caption: This hypothetical mechanism illustrates intermediate cancellation. Coefficients of the overall reaction do not generally give the measured reaction orders.
alt: Two steps A plus B to I and I plus B to P sum to A plus 2B to P. The slow first elementary step predicts a rate proportional to A and B, despite the overall coefficient 2 for B.

right: Forward rate = reverse rate
caption: At equilibrium each species is produced as quickly as it is consumed. Its concentration stays constant, but different species can have different concentrations.
alt: Opposing A to B and B to A arrows inside a closed boundary. Forward and reverse rate curves converge to the same nonzero rate.

left: Le Chatelier: partly oppose a stress
right: Separate the jump from the shift
caption: For this A ⇌ B example, adding A causes an immediate increase followed by partial consumption at fixed temperature and volume.
alt: Adding reactant A shifts A to B. Its concentration–time graph jumps upward, then falls to a new plateau above the initial concentration.

right: Temperature: identify the heat side
caption: Compression at fixed temperature favours fewer gas particles when gas coefficients differ. Heating favours the endothermic direction; cooling favours the exothermic direction.
alt: For nitrogen plus three hydrogen to two ammonia, compression favours the two-gas-particle product side. Heating an exothermic equilibrium shifts left and cooling shifts right.

right: Enthalpy and entropy tendencies
caption: The sketches illustrate an entropy trend, not a complete spontaneity test. When enthalpy and entropy tendencies oppose, temperature and their magnitudes matter.
alt: Ordered and dispersed arrangements of the same nine particles illustrate more accessible arrangements. Separate arrows show tendencies toward lower enthalpy and higher entropy.

right: Q tells the adjustment direction
caption: Use the same balanced expression for Q and K. Compare them at the same temperature; K alone says nothing about reaction speed.
alt: The ammonia equilibrium expression places squared ammonia over nitrogen times cubed hydrogen. A comparison line places Q below or above K with arrows toward equilibrium.

right: Solve and check the equilibrium
caption: This hypothetical starting mixture has 1.0 M each of H₂ and I₂ and no HI. The value of K is required to determine x.
alt: An ICE table for H2 plus I2 to 2HI has changes minus x, minus x and plus 2x. The resulting expression is K equals 4x squared divided by 1 minus x squared.

right: Saturation is a dynamic balance
caption: Ion and molecule sketches distinguish conductivity. In a saturated solution with excess solid, ions still exchange between the solid and solution.
alt: Mobile positive and negative ions are compared with neutral molecular solute. A saturated solution above excess solid has equal dissolution and crystallization directions.

right: Separate before the next ion test
caption: Use the textbook solubility table to choose reagents. A precipitate alone may fit more than one possible ion, so plan selective and confirmatory tests.
alt: A reagent is added to an unknown solution and a solid appears. A separation sequence shows selective reagent addition, filtration, then testing the remaining filtrate.

right: Build Ksp from the balanced equation
caption: The s and 2s relationships apply when PbCl₂ is the only source of its ions in initially pure water. A common ion requires an initial concentration term.
alt: One dissolved PbCl2 formula unit gives one lead ion and two chloride ions. Molar solubility s leads to Ksp equals s times 2s squared, or 4s cubed.

right: Compare the trial ion product to Ksp
caption: Assume additive solution volumes. First calculate each ion’s concentration after mixing, before precipitation; then evaluate Qsp using the salt’s stoichiometry.
alt: Separate silver and chloride solutions are mixed. Their diluted concentrations form Qsp, which is compared with Ksp for unsaturation, equilibrium threshold or precipitation.

right: Conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺
caption: These diagrams show proton transfer in water. They complement the Arrhenius definitions given above and explain how water can act as either acid or base.
alt: HA gives a proton to water, forming A minus and hydronium. The conjugate pairs HA/A minus and water/hydronium differ by exactly one proton and one charge unit.

left: Strong versus weak at the same C
right: Strength and concentration are distinct
caption: The particle models contain the same number of original acid units. The weak-acid ionization fraction is illustrative; it depends on Ka and concentration.
alt: Equal acid-unit counts show complete ionization for a strong acid and partial ionization for a weak acid. Labels distinguish strength from concentration and relate larger Ka to stronger acid.

left: Water produces both kinds of ion
right: At fixed temperature, Kw is constant
caption: Neutrality always means equal hydronium and hydroxide concentrations. The familiar 10⁻⁷ M values and neutral pH 7 apply at 25 °C.
alt: Autoionization of two waters gives hydronium and hydroxide. Both are 10 to the minus 7 M in neutral pure water at 25 degrees C; increasing one lowers the other at fixed Kw.

left: pH locates acidic, neutral and basic
right: A logarithmic step is a factor of ten
caption: Use the dilute-solution concentration approximation here. The 0–14 range is a familiar teaching scale, not an absolute limit; Kw changes with temperature.
alt: A pH scale marks acidic below 7, neutral at 7 and basic above 7 at 25 degrees C. Steps from pH 3 to 4 to 5 show hydronium dropping tenfold each step.

left: Ionization: x relative to starting C
right: The square-root shortcut needs a check
caption: This weak monoprotic acid model neglects water’s hydronium contribution. That requires x to be large compared with the hydronium from water.
alt: A weak-acid ICE relation gives remaining HA as C minus x and each ion as x. Ka equals x squared over C minus x, approximated by x squared over C only if x is small.

right: A weak acid’s conjugate base hydrolyzes
caption: Sodium acetate is the basic-salt example. Other salts can be acidic or neutral; amphiprotic ions and salts with two reactive ions need further comparison.
alt: Sodium acetate dissociates into spectator sodium and acetate, which accepts a proton from water and produces hydroxide, making the solution basic.

left: Buffer: a weak acid and its partner
right: Each partner removes an added reagent
caption: Buffering works while both components remain available. Do the neutralization mole calculation first; dilution lowers capacity even if the ratio changes little.
alt: A buffer contains a weak acid HA and conjugate base A minus. A minus consumes added hydronium, while HA consumes added hydroxide; their ratio affects pH and total amounts affect capacity.

right: Equivalence follows stoichiometry
caption: The equal cV relation shown is for a 1:1 reaction. Use the balanced mole ratio for other titrations. An indicator endpoint is an experimental approximation to equivalence.
alt: A burette of known titrant delivers drops to an analyte flask. A one-to-one HCl/NaOH reaction makes acid and base moles equal at equivalence, distinguished from the observed endpoint.

left: A titration curve shows changing species
right: One curve needs several pH models
caption: Schematic curve for a weak monoprotic acid titrated with a strong base at 25 °C. Half-equivalence gives pH ≈ pKa in the usual buffer approximation; equivalence is basic.
alt: A rising weak-acid strong-base titration curve marks half-equivalence at pH equal to pKa and equivalence above 7. The second panel assigns the appropriate calculation to each region.

right: Acidic anhydride: a non-metal example
caption: These are representative reactive oxides, not universal rules. Some metal and non-metal oxides are unreactive, insoluble, neutral or amphoteric.
alt: Sodium oxide reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide and a basic solution. Sulfur trioxide forms sulfuric acid, which ionizes to give an acidic solution.

right: The agent causes its partner’s change
caption: The zinc/copper-ion example shows coupled electron transfer. Oxidation numbers increase on oxidation and decrease on reduction.
alt: Zinc loses two electrons to become zinc 2 plus; copper 2 plus gains two electrons to become copper metal. Zinc is the reducing agent and copper ion is the oxidizing agent.

right: Balance atoms and charge in the medium
caption: The simple metal example cancels two electrons. Reactions containing oxygen and hydrogen also require the water/H⁺/OH⁻ steps appropriate to the medium.
alt: Zinc oxidation produces two electrons; two silver-ion reductions consume them, giving a balanced overall reaction. An acidic balancing guide uses water, hydrogen ions and electrons, then hydroxide for conversion to basic medium.

right: Subtract the two tabulated reductions
caption: Typical rounded Table A7 values are shown. The sign predicts standard-state thermodynamic direction; it does not establish a fast reaction.
alt: Copper reduction at plus 0.34 volts is compared with zinc reduction at minus 0.76 volts. Copper-ion reduction with zinc oxidation gives standard cell potential plus 1.10 volts.

right: Electrons in wire; ions in electrolyte
caption: Zinc/copper galvanic cell: electrons travel from the negative anode to the positive cathode. The salt bridge maintains charge balance by ion migration.
alt: Two half-cells are connected by an external wire and salt bridge. Electrons flow from zinc anode to copper cathode. Anions migrate toward the anode and cations toward the cathode.

right: Use electron stoichiometry and charge
caption: This is molten sodium chloride, so sodium forms at the cathode. Aqueous NaCl has different competing reactants and must be assessed separately using the book’s table notes.
alt: A DC supply connects positive anode and negative cathode in molten sodium chloride. Chloride is oxidized to chlorine and sodium ions are reduced to sodium. Charge equals current times time and electron moles equal charge over Faraday constant.
